mira.name: Mira
mira.greeting: You must be the new apprentice. I am Mira. I make maps of the Hollow, though the best way to learn a place is to walk it.
lines: The old gate leads to North Common and Cedar Rise. The mill bridge opens the Eastbank neighbourhood.
My cottage is up in North Common. You are welcome to visit. Each front door leads to its own home.
mira.prompt: What would you like to know?

topics.title: Tell me about your maps.
lines: A name is like a mark on a map: it gives you a useful way to refer to something.
In Python, a variable gives a value a name. I can keep a note in the notebook’s memory and find it again later.

lesson.title: A name for a place
lesson.explanation: The variable place_name holds a string. Saving it in world.memory keeps that small note after you Apply.

lines: Watch the race beside the old wheel: the pale foam follows the current.
There is more village beyond the mill yard now. My teal-roofed home is on the east bank.

topics.title: How do you repeat a task?
lines: A mill turns the same way again and again. I try to make my work just as steady.
A for loop repeats a small job for every item in a list. This example visits only the lamps your notebook already knows.

lesson.title: One task, many lamps
lesson.explanation: world.lamps contains lamps in places you have visited. The loop proposes lighting each one. Run previews those changes; only Apply makes them real.

bram.name: Bram
bram.greeting: Hello! I am Bram. Timber, doors, stubborn chairs: that is my trade.
lines: A house can change its place without losing what is inside. Try the builder when you want to settle in.
My workshop is just behind me. Come in from the front doorstep.
bram.prompt: What would you like to know?

topics.title: How do you reuse a good pattern?
lines: Once I have a pattern that fits, I give it a name and use it again. A chair is easier when every leg follows the same plan.
A Python function is a named piece of work. Give it an input, and it can return a useful result.

lesson.title: A reusable maker’s mark
lesson.explanation: label_for takes a name and returns a label. program calls that helper, then stores the result in your notebook’s memory.

lines: The northern paths are quiet. Follow them to the cedars and you will find Nell.
I keep my home here on North Common. You can always come by for a rest.

topics.title: How do you keep track of seeds?
lines: I keep seeds together in little trays. A list does much the same thing: several things, kept in order.
Square brackets make a Python list. Here I keep three plant names together in the notebook’s memory.

lesson.title: A tray of names
lesson.explanation: The list seeds contains three strings in order. Lists can be saved in world.memory, then read by another program after you Apply.

nell.name: Nell
nell.greeting: Welcome, dear. Nell is my name. The Hollow is growing again.
lines: Every home has its own little world. Your notebook remembers the room you are in.
The mist at the old trail keeps folk away from the deep woods. There is plenty to explore on this side.

topics.title: How do you choose what to use?
lines: First I look at what I have. Then I choose. There is no sense reaching for a leaf that is not in the basket.
An if statement chooses a branch when a condition is true. Else gives us another path when it is false.

lesson.title: A choice from the basket
lesson.explanation: The condition checks whether sage is in the list. Exactly one branch stores a name in world.memory. This is a small example of making a choice in code.
